title: Your Chai Just Got Cheaper: India Wins Zero-Duty Tea Access to America
excerpt: A tariff breakthrough gives Indian tea exporters an edge over China just as a wave of Asian tea brands floods the US market.
body:
For decades, a cup of chai in America has been a story of cultural translation — the spiced milk tea of Indian railway platforms reimagined as a syrupy "chai latte" at Starbucks, the word itself stripped of meaning and doubled into the redundant "chai tea." But a quiet shift in trade policy may be about to make the real thing far more accessible.

Under the interim trade agreement framework being finalised between India and the United States, Indian teas are set to receive zero-duty access to the American market — a sharp reversal from the 50 per cent tariffs that hammered Indian tea exporters last year and sent shockwaves through an industry that considers America a key growth frontier.

## The Tariff Rollercoaster

The relief comes after a bruising year. When the US imposed sweeping 50 per cent tariffs on Indian goods in 2025, tea exporters were caught in the crossfire. Orders were cancelled. Shipments halted. Indian tea exports to the US, which typically run at 18 to 20 million kilograms annually, fell to just 15.2 million kilograms.

"In 2025, the quantity of export fell as after the stiff 50 per cent tariffs were imposed, Indian exporters halted shipments for some periods," Anshuman Kanoria, chairman of the Indian Tea Exporters Association, told *The Hindu Business Line*. "Now, we can go back to 18-20 million kgs because of the zero-duty on Indian tea exports."

The deal also hands India a crucial competitive advantage over China, its main rival in the American tea market. While the broader India-US trade pact remains in final negotiations — with India seeking tariff rates lower than those imposed on other Asian economies — tea appears to be one of the early beneficiaries.

## The Chinese Tea Invasion

The timing could not be more significant. The American tea market is in the middle of a massive land grab, with well-funded Chinese bubble tea chains like Chagee, Mixue, and others aggressively expanding into US cities. Chagee, which listed on the NASDAQ in April, has over 80 personnel working on its American expansion and plans to open a flagship store in the heart of Silicon Valley. The company's US executive, Emily Chang, a former Starbucks China executive, has described a plan to "promote tea among US consumers and establish it as a new product category" — effectively doing for tea what Starbucks did for coffee in China.

Meanwhile, US-born chains like Feng Cha are gearing up for the competition. "We're not trying to be like these national brands that want to go into fancy plazas and malls," says Feng Cha CEO Michael Gao, who has positioned the chain as a community-focused alternative with deep roots in Texas.

## What This Means for NRIs

For the Indian diaspora, the zero-duty access is about more than economics. It is about identity. The tea that Indians drink — strong, spiced, boiled with milk and sugar in a way that would horrify a British tea purist — has never quite found its commercial footing in the American market. What exists is mostly an approximation: chai concentrates in cartons, powdered mixes in coffee shops, or the occasional cutting chai at an Indian grocery store.

But a new generation of Indian tea brands is pushing to change that. Vahdam Teas, a direct-from-India brand with global distribution, has built a premium positioning around single-estate teas and masala chai blends. The Chai Box, a US-based company, specialises in chai concentrates designed to taste like the real thing. Both stand to benefit from lower tariffs that make Indian teas more competitive against the flood of Chinese alternatives.

## The Bigger Picture

The tea tariff is a small but revealing piece of the broader India-US trade puzzle. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal has said the two countries are "very close" to finalising a comprehensive trade deal, following talks with US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in New Delhi this week. Under the initial framework agreed in February, India secured an 18 per cent tariff rate — lower than competing economies like Bangladesh and Vietnam — in exchange for lowering trade barriers and purchasing more American goods.

But the deal has been complicated by the US Supreme Court's invalidation of certain sweeping tariffs and a continuing Section 301 probe into alleged labour practices in India.

For NRIs, the practical implication is straightforward: the Indian teas and spice blends that stock the shelves of Patel Brothers, India Bazaar, and dozens of online retailers should become easier and cheaper to import. In a country where 80 per cent of tea consumption is iced or ready-to-drink, the real opportunity may lie in convincing Americans that the best chai in the world comes not from a syrup pump in a coffee shop, but from a steel pot on an Indian stove.
